title: Who owns this String

prereqs.why: The exercise is written entirely around which function takes ownership and which only borrows, and what the caller may do afterwards.
You already know what a function with parameters and a return value is; what changes in Rust is what passing one means.

statement:
Read lines of input until it runs out. Skip blank lines. For each non-blank
line, trim the surrounding whitespace to get a `word`, and then use three
functions on it in this order:

```rust
fn measure(s: &String) -> usize   // borrows: caller keeps the String
fn shout(mut s: String) -> String // takes it, uppercases it, gives it back
fn consume(s: String) -> usize    // takes it for good
```

Print, per line of input:

```
measured <len> <len>        measure called twice on the same String
shout <THE UPPERCASED WORD>
consumed <len>
```

```
input:   cache               output:  measured 5 5
         Ring                         shout CACHE
                                      consumed 5
                                      measured 4 4
                                      shout RING
                                      consumed 4
```

### The point of the problem

In Rust, a `String` has exactly **one owner**, and the owner is responsible for
freeing it. So these two lines mean different things:

```rust
let n = measure(&word);      // borrow: word is still yours afterwards
let len = consume(word);     // move:  word is gone, you cannot touch it again
```

After the move, using `word` is a **compile error**, not a crash:

```
error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `word`
  |
  |     let len = consume(word);
  |                       ---- value moved here
  |     println!("{}", word);
  |                    ^^^^ value borrowed here after move
```

That error is the entire feature. In C++ the same program compiles and runs, and
whether it works depends on whether anything freed the buffer yet.

### The order matters, so write it in this order

`measure` twice, then `shout`, then `consume`. Each step is only possible
because of what the previous one did or did not take:

- `measure` borrows, so calling it twice is fine and `word` survives
- `shout` **takes** `word` and returns a new owner - so the result has to be
  bound to a name, and `word` is unusable from then on
- `consume` takes that, and nothing is usable afterwards

If you try to call `measure(&word)` after `shout(word)`, the compiler will stop
you. Do it once deliberately, read the error, then put it back.

### Boundary cases

Blank lines and lines of only spaces, which are skipped. A line that is already
uppercase, which `shout` leaves unchanged. Lines with inner spaces - only the
*surrounding* whitespace is trimmed, so `two words` stays one `word` of 9
characters. Empty input, which prints nothing. A line with digits and
punctuation, which uppercasing leaves alone.

### Platform assumptions

Input is ASCII, and `make_ascii_uppercase` only changes `a-z`. `len()` on a
`String` is the length in **bytes**, not characters - for ASCII they are the
same, and the solution says what happens when they are not. Lines are at most
200 bytes and there are at most 200 of them.
hints: `input.lines()` yields `&str` borrowed from the input buffer. `line.trim().to_string()` makes an owned `String` from it - `trim` returns a borrowed sub-slice, and `to_string` copies it into a new allocation you own.

`shout` needs `mut s: String` in its signature. That `mut` is not part of the type - it says the parameter binding is mutable inside the function, which is what lets you call `make_ascii_uppercase` on it. The caller does not need `word` to be `mut`.

Bind the result: `let loud = shout(word);`. Writing just `shout(word);` and then using `word` is the error worth reading - the value moved into the function and came back out as a return value you discarded.

cases.expect:
measured 5 5
shout CACHE
consumed 5
measured 4 4
shout RING
consumed 4
